Say the whole slide.
column2:
Good morning.
My name is Martin Maxa, and I'm from the Czech Technical University in Prague, the Faculty of Electrical Engineering.
This is joint work with my colleagues Jakub Svatoš and Jakub Zelinka.
Today I'll show you a small neural network that recognizes the sound of an artillery launch.
It runs on a cheap microcontroller, and it keeps working in noise.

Slide 2 – Motivation and research questions [0:40–1:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Let me start with the motivation.
Recent conflicts have shown that we need cheap systems that can warn about artillery fire.
Acoustic sensing is a good candidate.
It is passive, it needs little power, and it doesn't send out any signal, so it is hard to find.
But a real sensor has two problems at the same time.
It has to work in noise.
And it has to run on small, low-power hardware.
[CLICK]
So we ask two questions.
First – to make the classifier robust to noise, is it enough to add noise to the features, or do we have to add it to the audio signal itself?
And second – does this robustness survive when we quantize the model and run it on a microcontroller?

Slide 3 – Two-stage detection pipeline [1:50–2:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Our system has two stages.
The first stage is a streaming trigger.
It listens all the time and looks for impulsive events.
It is our earlier work – it detected all the gunshots we tested, and it works down to a signal-to-noise ratio of five decibels.
The second stage is what this talk is about.
For each candidate, we cut a sixty millisecond window around the peak, compute MFCC features, and a small CNN decides: artillery launch, or not.
So to be clear – we evaluate only the second stage.
We assume the trigger has already found the event.

Slide 4 – Field recordings [2:50–3:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
The data come from real artillery measurements.
This is our recording station.
Four synchronized microphones on one mount, an audio interface and a laptop.
We recorded for two days, with one type of gun – a 152 millimetre self-propelled howitzer.
The station was one to two kilometres from the impact area, and the guns fired from about five to ten kilometres away.
On the right is one launch.
Below it, you can see the sixty millisecond window that the classifier actually sees.
Thirty percent of it is before the peak, and seventy percent after it.

Slide 5 – Labelled corpus and event-level split [3:50–4:40]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This is the whole labelled corpus – eight hundred and forty-one events.
Fifty of them are artillery launches.
The rest are things that can also fire the trigger – doors, shouts, bells, and small-arms gunshots.
The gunshots are the hard cases, because they are impulsive too.
We split the data by event, not by recording.
So the four channels of one shot are never in training and test at the same time.
In training we use all four channels, and a class-weighted loss for the imbalance.
The test set has ten launches and one hundred and fifty-eight other events.

column2: The test set has ten launches and one hundred and fifty-eight other events.

column1:
Slide 6 – MFCC front end and compact CNN [4:40–5:40]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Now the method.
From each window we compute MFCCs.
We use very short frames – two and a half milliseconds, with a one millisecond step – because the event is short and changes fast.
We keep twelve coefficients, so each event becomes a small matrix, fifty-eight by twelve.
The classifier is a small CNN.
Two convolution blocks, each with max pooling, then one dense layer with dropout, and a sigmoid output.
In total it has about seventy-two thousand parameters.
That is small enough for a microcontroller.

column2: That is small enough for a microcontroller.

column1:
Slide 7 – Two ways to train for noise [5:40–6:40]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
To make the network robust, we add noise during training.
And there are two places where we can add it.
Option A: we compute the MFCCs once, and then add small random noise directly to the feature matrix.
This is cheap and simple.
Option B: we add noise to the audio signal first, and only then compute the MFCCs.
This costs more, because we have to recompute the features every time.
The question is whether A is good enough.
Noise in the audio does not stay simple after the MFCC – it changes the features in a nonlinear way.
So A may not look like real noise at all.

column1:
Slide 7 – Two ways to train for noise
Last sentence (the bridge to the next slide)?
column2: So A may not look like real noise at all.

column1:
Slide 8 – Evaluation protocol [6:40–7:30]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
How do we test it?
We take the held-out test set and add noise to the audio – again before the MFCC, because that's what happens in the real sensor.
The noise level is set per event, from the power of the event itself.
We test thirty, twenty, ten and five decibels.
And then zero and minus five, which is already beyond what the trigger can handle.
Every number is an average over twenty-five runs – five training seeds and five noise seeds.
And we report mainly the MCC, because the classes are imbalanced.

Slide 8 – Evaluation protocol

column2: And we report mainly the MCC, because the classes are imbalanced.

column1:
Slide 9 – Result 1 – where to add the noise [7:30–8:40]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This is the first result.
Same network, trained three times – only the augmentation is different.
The light grey line is option A, noise on the features.
It is fine on clean data, but it falls apart in noise.
At five decibels the MCC is only zero point three.
The red line is option B, noise on the waveform.
It stays almost flat – zero point nine eight even at five decibels.
And the surprise is the middle line.
When we combine both, it is worse than B alone.
So feature noise is not just insufficient – here it actually hurts.

Slide 9 – Result 1 – where to add the noise

column2: So feature noise is not just insufficient – here it actually hurts.

column1:
Slide 10 – Result 2 – held-out robustness of the deployed model [8:40–9:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Now the deployed model in more detail.
In the trained range, from clean down to five decibels, the MCC stays between zero point nine eight and zero point nine nine.
In the grey area, beyond what the trigger can handle, it goes down slowly.
Zero point nine five at zero decibels, and zero point eight three at minus five.
But look at how it fails.
Precision stays at one.
Only recall drops.
So in very strong noise the model misses some launches – but it does not give false alarms.
And no small-arms gunshot was ever classified as artillery.
Quantization to int8 made no real difference.

Slide 10 – Result 2 – held-out robustness of the deployed model
Last sentence (the bridge to the next slide)?
column2: Quantization to int8 made no real difference.

column1:
Slide 11 – Result 3 – on the ESP32-S3 [9:50–10:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Finally, the microcontroller.
We sent all test inputs to the ESP32-S3, at all noise levels – that's one thousand one hundred and seventy-six inferences.
One thousand one hundred and seventy-one gave exactly the same result as the PC.
The other five had a score of exactly zero point five, right on the decision boundary, where a one-bit rounding difference can flip the answer.
One inference takes thirty-two milliseconds.
Please note, that's only the network – the MFCCs were computed on the host.
The model has about eighty kilobytes, and the whole firmware needs less than one hundred and fifty kilobytes of RAM.

Slide 12 – Limitations [10:50–11:20]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Of course, there are limitations.
We evaluate only the classifier, not the full stream.
We have only fifty launches, and one type of gun.
And the noise is synthetic.
So these are the next steps for us.

Last sentence (the bridge to the next slide)?

column1:
Slide 13 – Conclusion [11:20–12:00]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
To sum up.
A small CNN with seventy-two thousand parameters works well as the second stage of an artillery launch detector.
If you want it robust to noise, add the noise to the audio, not to the features.
Feature noise fails, and combined with waveform noise it even makes things worse.
Our model keeps an MCC of zero point nine eight at five decibels, and it runs on an ESP32-S3 in thirty-two milliseconds.
Thank you for your attention.
I'm happy to take your questions.
